newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservatives seek scapegoat as defeat looms.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservatives seek scapegoat as defeat looms.

text.p: With just a handful of results in from Britain's election, recriminations were already flying in the Conservative Party on Friday as it faced the prospect of being cast into the wilderness after 18 years in power.

With exit polls predicting a landslide for Tony Blair's Labour Party, a parade of senior Conservative figures were analysing their election campaign before the televison cameras and finding it seriously lacking.
"There will have to be a lot of questions asked and answers to give," Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine told BBC radio.
"I think that the campaign had a lack of focus and a lack of clarity about the message," said former party chairman Norman Tebbit.

Tebbit, a right-winger close to former premier Margaret Thatcher, was quick to blame Prime Minister John Major, the dominant figure in the Conservative campaign, for not taking into account the strength of opposition within his party to closer links with Europe.
"If he (Major) had led that change of view in the party, the view of the great mass of the people, he would have stood a very good chance of winning the election," Tebbit said.
Party maverick Edwina Currie decried the six-week campaign battle against a rejuvenated Labour Party as "a shambles".

Several senior figures said the divisions over Europe had turned off the electorate. Eurosceptics had demanded Major rule out joining a single European currency but Major stuck to his "wait and see" policy.
In the most dramatic moment of the campaign, Major appealed to Eurosceptics in his party not to tie his hands in negotiations on the single currency.
"Obviously any party that gives the impression of not being united, that cannot help you in an election," said Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind.
Defence Secretary Michael Portillo, who is expected to be the main leadership contender from the right wing of the party if Major stands down, said a battle to unite the party was ahead.
"I hope that we should do it in a considered, measured way in a period of time, without damaging the unity of the party," Portillo told the BBC.
Portillo is expected to be among the first to call for Major's head if the party suffers the kind of defeat polls are predicting. Analysts said resignation calls were inevitable.

If the Conservatives suffer a defeat as great as the exit polls indicate, the Eurosceptics who have battled Major's "wait and see" line on closer links with the European Union would be strengthened, said Professor Ivor Crewe of Essex University.
"Everyone will be competing for the support of the right-wing Conservatives, the right wing will have nothing to do but be courted," Crewe told Reuters.
But analysts also warned the party could become even more bitterly divided if Major bowed to pressure to resign quickly.
"There is fear that if they go for someone divisive they will lose part of the party," said Crewe.
He said it was not inevitable that Major would go.
"You can't take it for granted, even if they lose badly, that Major will resign. He is not obliged to resign. There is no tradition in the party to resign immediately."
Heseltine, who himself stood as a leadership candidate against Margaret Thatcher in 1990, called for a "mature period of reflection" and said he would back Major in any contest.
